To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) eliminating small magnitude components from high-dimensional vectors is a poor proxy for eliminating gradients with relatively low magnitude; (b) eliminating small magnitude weight and activation components is a good proxy for eliminating gradients; (c) training with small magnitude components eliminated is faster and yields better accuracy than training with gradients with small magnitudes eliminated.

(i) the magnitude of a vector component is not a good proxy for its impact on a high-dimensional vector; (ii) eliminating small magnitude components from weight and activation vectors is a better approach for training CNNs than eliminating small magnitude components in gradients; and (iii) SWAT reduces computations and memory footprint for training CNNs by eliminating small magnitude components during forward and backward propagation, while maintaining or improving accuracy.

we propose Sparse Weight Activation training (SWAT), a method that reduces the memory and computation demands of training CNNs by eliminating small magnitude components from weight and activation vectors.

the problem of training a deep convolutional neural network.

we show that training CNNs can be done with significantly reduced memory and computational demands with better accuracy.

SWAT reduces training time by 50% while improving accuracy and memory efficiency by up to 80%.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the direction of high dimensional vectors is more important than the magnitude of individual components when considering the direction of the vector.
we can train deeper networks on larger datasets using less computation by eliminating small magnitude components from weight and activation vectors.
the magnitude of a gradient does not necessarily indicate its importance to the training process.
